questions.question: When is a percutaneous renal tumor core biopsy clinically indicated and recommended in a patient with a renal mass?
options: Before every planned surgical partial or radical nephrectomy to confirm malignancy
To evaluate purely cystic, fluid-filled lesions like classic Bosniak Class I cysts
Before active surveillance, tumor ablation, or systemic therapy when no prior pathological diagnosis is available
Only after the patient has failed at least three cycles of systemic chemotherapy
questions.answerText: Before active surveillance, tumor ablation, or systemic therapy when no prior pathological diagnosis is available
questions.explanation: Renal tumor biopsy is not mandatory before every surgically managed enhancing mass [34, 35]. However, it is strongly recommended before tumor ablation or systemic therapy (when no previous pathology exists), and is useful in selected active-surveillance or indeterminate cases [11, 35, 36]. Biopsies of purely cystic lesions (like Bosniak I) should be avoided unless a solid component is present [34, 37].

questions.question: Which of the following depth boundaries is the most critical factor in determining the therapeutic pathway for bladder cancer, dividing the disease spectrum into two fundamentally different management strategies?
options: Invasion of the lamina propria (T1 vs. Ta)
Invasion of the detrusor muscle (T1 vs. T2)
Invasion of the perivesical fat (T2 vs. T3)
Invasion of the pelvic or abdominal wall (T3 vs. T4)
questions.answerText: Invasion of the detrusor muscle (T1 vs. T2)
questions.explanation: The sources emphasize that the distinction between **T1 (invading lamina propria)** and **T2 (invading muscularis propria/detrusor muscle)** is clinically critical because the depth of muscle invasion changes management completely [1-4]. Ta, Tis, and T1 are managed as **Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (NMIBC)** with organ-preservation strategies, whereas T2 or higher is managed as **Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer (MIBC)**, requiring aggressive curative interventions [1-3].

questions.question: Which of the following is considered an established risk factor for bladder Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) but is NOT historically considered a direct risk factor for standard Transitional Cell (Urothelial) Carcinoma?
options: Cigarette smoking
Exposure to aromatic amines/aniline dyes
Chronic bladder schistosomiasis (bilharziasis) infection
Prior cyclophosphamide chemotherapy exposure
questions.answerText: Chronic bladder schistosomiasis (bilharziasis) infection
questions.explanation: The sources explicitly highlight that **schistosomiasis (bilharziasis) predisposes patients mainly to Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)** due to chronic mechanical irritation, abnormal tryptophan metabolism, and bacterial ammonia production [5-8]. In contrast, classic transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma risk is driven by smoking, pelvic irradiation, cyclophosphamide, and occupational chemical exposure [5, 8-10].

questions.question: A 65-year-old male patient undergoes a Transurethral Resection of a Bladder Tumor (TURBT). Pathological analysis reveals a high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma, but the pathologist notes that no detrusor muscle is present in the specimen. According to guidelines, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Initiate immediate radical cystectomy
Perform a repeat TURBT within 2 to 6 weeks to ensure correct staging and eliminate residual disease
Start intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy without further surgery
Place the patient on active surveillance cystoscopy every 6 months
questions.answerText: Perform a repeat TURBT within 2 to 6 weeks to ensure correct staging and eliminate residual disease
questions.explanation: A complete TURBT with **detrusor muscle present in the specimen** is essential to confirm that the tumor has not invaded the muscle [11, 12]. The sources state that a **repeat TURBT is indicated within 2–6 weeks** if the initial resection is incomplete, if detrusor muscle is absent (except for selected low-grade Ta tumors), or if T1 disease is diagnosed [11, 13]. This helps to improve staging accuracy and reduces residual disease [13].

questions.question: Based on the past exam questions and the clinical management matrix, what is the standard, standard-of-care curative treatment for a patient diagnosed with Stage T2b (muscle-invasive) bladder cancer?
options: Transurethral resection (TURBT) alone
Radical cystectomy
Systemic chemotherapy alone
Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) instillation
questions.answerText: Radical cystectomy
questions.explanation: According to the past undergraduate examinations and clinical guidelines, the **standard treatment for stage T2b (and T2 in general) bladder cancer is a radical cystectomy** [14-20]. For eligible patients, radical cystectomy is routinely preceded by neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy [2, 12, 14].

questions.question: A 63-year-old male is diagnosed with bladder cancer invading the perivesical fat, staged as T3 N0 M0. Based on past urology board examinations, which of the following is the best therapeutic option?
options: Radical cystectomy
Partial cystectomy
Radiotherapy
Systemic chemotherapy alone
BCG instillation in the bladder
questions.answerText: Radical cystectomy
questions.explanation: This question directly replicates a recurring past exam question in the sources: a **63-year-old male diagnosed with stage T3 bladder cancer is best treated by radical cystectomy** [21-25]. Standard management for operable, locally advanced MIBC (such as T3) comprises radical cystectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection, frequently combined with perioperative chemotherapy [14, 19].

questions.question: Which of the following options represents the gold-standard, first-line adjuvant treatment for high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) or carcinoma in situ (Tis) to reduce progression and recurrence?
options: Immediate systemic platinum-based combination chemotherapy
Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy
Immediate radical pelvic exenteration
External beam pelvic radiotherapy
questions.answerText: Intravesical Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy
questions.explanation: The sources confirm that **intravesical BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) is the gold standard** and first-line treatment for high-risk NMIBC, carcinoma in situ (CIS), and high-grade T1 tumors [12, 26-30]. BCG acts as an immunotherapy, stimulating a local immune response that destroys residual cancer cells, thereby significantly reducing both recurrence and progression rates [30].

questions.question: Following a radical cystectomy, which of the following lists of clinical factors must be evaluated to determine a patient's suitability for an orthotopic neobladder rather than an ileal conduit?
options: None; orthotopic neobladder is the universal standard for all patients undergoing cystectomy.
Renal and hepatic function, urethral tumor involvement, severe bowel disease, and patient cognition/dexterity.
Prostate volume, history of nephrolithiasis, and presence of microscopic hematuria.
Patient age alone, with a strict cutoff at 50 years of age.
questions.answerText: Renal and hepatic function, urethral tumor involvement, severe bowel disease, and patient cognition/dexterity.
questions.explanation: The sources state that urinary diversion selection is highly individualized, and **orthotopic neobladder is not suitable for every patient** [31, 32]. Suitability depends on **renal and hepatic function, urethral tumor involvement, pre-existing bowel disease, patient cognition, and physical dexterity** to manage voiding mechanisms and potential metabolic or retention complications [31].

questions.question: Regarding the clinical presentation of urinary bladder carcinoma, which of the following statements represents an incorrect legacy concept or diagnostic trap?
options: Bladder cancer is usually painless, especially in its early stages.
The presence of painful hematuria is more characteristic of stones or acute infection rather than early malignancy.
Bladder cancer is usually highly painful and symptomatic in its early, localized stages.
Visible, painless, total hematuria with blood clots is the classic hallmark presentation.
questions.answerText: Bladder cancer is usually highly painful and symptomatic in its early, localized stages.
questions.explanation: According to the sources, early bladder cancer has **no abnormal physical findings and is characteristically painless** [33-35]. Painful hematuria is typical for stones or infection [36], whereas **painless visible hematuria** in an adult is the classic presentation of bladder cancer and must be considered malignant until proven otherwise [34, 35, 37, 38]. Pain is usually a sign of advanced, locally invasive, or metastatic disease [35, 36].

questions.question: Based on the clinical anatomy and past exams, which of the following statements about non-bilharzial bladder cancer is UNTRUE?
options: It is most commonly a transitional-cell (urothelial) carcinoma.
It occurs most frequently in the fundus (vault) of the bladder.
It usually presents as a cauliflower-like (papillary) mass.
It frequently manifests as painless hematuria.
questions.answerText: It occurs most frequently in the fundus (vault) of the bladder.
questions.explanation: This replicates a classic past exam question in the sources: it is **untrue that non-bilharzial bladder cancer occurs most frequently in the fundus** [39]. Non-bilharzial urothelial carcinoma typically arises from the lateral walls or base/trigone of the bladder [39]. The other choices (most commonly transitional-cell carcinoma, presenting as a cauliflower-like/papillary mass, and presenting as painless hematuria) are true statements [39].

questions.question: Which of the following chemotherapy agents is associated with a significantly increased risk of developing urothelial bladder cancer, and what is the underlying mechanism of this toxicity?
options: Cisplatin; direct renal tubular ischemia
Methotrexate; folic acid pathway antagonism in mucosal cells
Cyclophosphamide; excretion of its metabolite (acrolein) which directly damages the urothelium
Doxorubicin; cardiotoxicity transmitting venous backpressure to the pelvis
questions.answerText: Cyclophosphamide; excretion of its metabolite (acrolein) which directly damages the urothelium
questions.explanation: The sources state that **cyclophosphamide increases the risk of bladder cancer because of its metabolite (acrolein)** [40]. Acrolein is excreted in the urine, where it comes into direct contact with and damages the urothelial lining of the bladder, inducing severe irritation, hemorrhagic cystitis, and long-term carcinogenic changes [8, 40, 41].

questions.question: According to McNeal's zonal anatomy of the prostate, where do the majority of prostatic acinar adenocarcinomas arise, and how does this affect clinical detection on Digital Rectal Examination (DRE)?
options: Over 70% arise in the transition zone; they are easily palpable on DRE from the rectal wall.
Over 70% arise in the peripheral zone; their posterior location makes them accessible to palpation on DRE, though a normal exam does not exclude cancer.
Approximately 25% arise in the central zone; they are highly aggressive and always cause early urinary outflow obstruction.
Over 90% arise in the periurethral glands; they present as a soft, boggy, exquisitely tender mass on DRE.
questions.answerText: Over 70% arise in the peripheral zone; their posterior location makes them accessible to palpation on DRE, though a normal exam does not exclude cancer.
questions.explanation: The sources state that the majority of prostate cancers (70–75%) arise in the peripheral zone (PZ), which comprises the lateral, posterior, and apical surfaces of the gland [1-3]. Due to their posterior location, they can be palpable on digital rectal examination (DRE) as a hard, irregular nodule or induration [1, 4]. However, because many early cancers are clinically inapparent or located out of reach, a normal DRE does not exclude malignancy [1].

questions.question: According to the modern EAU 2026 early detection guidelines, what is the recommended starting age for risk-adapted PSA screening in a well-informed man carrying a known BRCA2 germline mutation?
options: From age 50
From age 45
From age 40
From age 35
questions.answerText: From age 40
questions.explanation: The EAU 2026 early detection guidelines recommend a risk-adapted approach for well-informed men with a life expectancy of at least 10–15 years: starting at age 50 for average-risk men, at age 45 for men of African descent or those with a family history of prostate cancer diagnosed before age 60, and at age 40 for men who carry pathogenic BRCA2 germline mutations [5, 6].

questions.question: In a 58-year-old man who is found to have an elevated serum Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) level of 6.2 ng/mL on a routine health check, what is the standard recommended first step before proceeding to a prostate biopsy?
options: Immediate transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) systematic 12-core biopsy.
Radical prostatectomy because a PSA > 4 ng/mL confirms malignancy.
Exclude confounding factors (such as UTI), repeat the PSA assay to verify elevation, and if persistent, obtain a multiparametric MRI (mpMRI).
Perform an urgent bone scintigraphy (bone scan) to rule out osteoblastic metastases.
questions.answerText: Exclude confounding factors (such as UTI), repeat the PSA assay to verify elevation, and if persistent, obtain a multiparametric MRI (mpMRI).
questions.explanation: Modern guidelines emphasize that PSA is continuous and not a cancer-specific yes/no test [6]. For asymptomatic patients with moderately elevated PSA (e.g., 3–10 ng/mL), clinicians should first verify the elevation with a repeat PSA assay, rule out clinical confounders like urinary tract infections (UTI) or prostatitis, and then obtain a multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) before initiating a biopsy to localize suspect lesions and score them using PI-RADS v2.1 [6-10].

questions.question: When performing a prostate biopsy guided by mpMRI-ultrasound fusion, which biopsy route is increasingly favored in contemporary clinical practice, and what is the primary clinical advantage of this route?
options: The transrectal route, because it completely avoids the need for local anesthesia.
The transperineal route, because it significantly reduces the risk of post-procedural infectious complications and sepsis.
The transurethral route, because it allows simultaneous resection of the transition zone.
The transvesical route, because it provides the best exposure of the central zone.
questions.answerText: The transperineal route, because it significantly reduces the risk of post-procedural infectious complications and sepsis.
questions.explanation: Modern guidelines state that the transperineal route is increasingly preferred over the transrectal route for prostate biopsies [8, 11, 12]. This preference is driven by the significantly lower risk of infectious complications and post-procedural sepsis associated with the transperineal approach [8, 11, 12].

questions.question: A pathologist reports a prostate needle-core biopsy as containing adenocarcinoma with a Gleason Score of 4 + 3 = 7. According to the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) consensus terminology, which Grade Group (GG) does this represent?
options: Grade Group 2 (GG2)
Grade Group 3 (GG3)
Grade Group 4 (GG4)
Grade Group 5 (GG5)
questions.answerText: Grade Group 3 (GG3)
questions.explanation: The modern ISUP classification system groups Gleason scores into five Grade Groups: GG1 corresponds to Gleason 3+3=6; GG2 is Gleason 3+4=7 (predominantly pattern 3); GG3 is Gleason 4+3=7 (predominantly pattern 4); GG4 is Gleason 8 (4+4, 3+5, or 5+3); and GG5 is Gleason 9 or 10 [1, 13]. Gleason 4+3 is unfavorable intermediate-risk and corresponds to Grade Group 3 [13, 14].

questions.question: According to current NCCN/EAU risk stratification, which clinical profile defines "Low-Risk" localized prostate cancer?
options: PSA 10–20 ng/mL, Grade Group 2 (Gleason 3+4), and clinical stage cT2b
PSA < 10 ng/mL, Grade Group 1 (Gleason 6), and clinical stage cT1c to cT2a
PSA > 20 ng/mL, Grade Group 4 (Gleason 8), and clinical stage cT3a
Any PSA level, Grade Group 3 (Gleason 4+3), and clinical stage cT2c
questions.answerText: PSA < 10 ng/mL, Grade Group 1 (Gleason 6), and clinical stage cT1c to cT2a
questions.explanation: The risk stratification tables in the sources define the Low-Risk category as having a serum PSA < 10 ng/mL, an ISUP Grade Group 1 (Gleason 3+3=6), and a clinical stage of cT1c to cT2a [13]. Active surveillance is the primary standard-of-care strategy for these patients if life expectancy exceeds 10 years [12, 15].

questions.question: What is the key difference in intent and monitoring between Active Surveillance (AS) and Watchful Waiting (WW) for prostate cancer?
options: AS is palliative and utilizes no serial imaging, whereas WW is curative and requires repeat biopsies every 6 months.

AS is a curative-intent strategy that defers active treatment in low-risk patients while preserving a curative window through structured monitoring (serial PSA, MRI, repeat biopsies); whereas WW is a palliative conservative strategy for patients with limited life expectancy or major comorbidities, focusing on symptom-directed follow-up.
AS is reserved for metastatic disease to monitor hormonal resistance, while WW is used exclusively in patients carrying the BRCA2 mutation who are under 40.
There is no clinical distinction; both terms refer to the immediate initiation of low-dose bilateral orchiectomy.
questions.answerText: AS is a curative-intent strategy that defers active treatment in low-risk patients while preserving a curative window through structured monitoring (serial PSA, MRI, repeat biopsies); whereas WW is a palliative conservative strategy for patients with limited life expectancy or major comorbidities, focusing on symptom-directed follow-up.
questions.explanation: The sources contrast active surveillance and watchful waiting [16, 17]. Active surveillance is designed to defer or avoid immediate treatment in low-risk or selected favorable intermediate-risk patients with >10-year life expectancy, utilizing structured monitoring (PSA, MRI, digital exams, repeat biopsies) to trigger curative intervention if reclassification occurs [15, 16]. Watchful waiting is a palliative conservative strategy for older or frail patients with limited life expectancy, where follow-up is clinical and intervention is triggered only by symptoms or complications [14, 16].

questions.question: What is the current standard of care for a fit patient presenting with de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) according to modern guidelines?
options: Immediate radical prostatectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection alone without any systemic therapy.
Systemic androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) monotherapy, as combination therapy has been shown to offer no survival advantage.
Intensified systemic therapy combining androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI), with or without docetaxel.
High-dose oral estrogens combined with systemic cyclophosphamide chemotherapy.
questions.answerText: Intensified systemic therapy combining androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI), with or without docetaxel.
questions.explanation: Modern guidelines state that for fit patients with de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, ADT monotherapy is no longer the standard [18, 19]. Instead, combination systemic therapy is standard: combining ADT (castration) with an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI), with docetaxel used as part of selected triplet regimens, because this combination therapy significantly improves survival [11, 17-19].

questions.question: Prostate cancer is highly bone-tropic. Which of the following represents the most common site for distant hematogenous metastasis and the classic radiographic type of these bone lesions?
options: Long bones of the lower extremity; presenting as purely osteolytic lesions.
The skull; presenting as mixed lytic-blastic lesions with high serum alpha-fetoprotein.
The vertebral column (spine) and pelvis; presenting as characteristically osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions.
The ribs and sternum; presenting as purely osteolytic lesions similar to renal cell carcinoma.
questions.answerText: The vertebral column (spine) and pelvis; presenting as characteristically osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions.
questions.explanation: The sources state that the most common site for distant prostate cancer metastasis is bone—specifically the vertebral column (spine) and pelvis [7, 20-22]. Furthermore, past surgical board and undergraduate examinations highlight that while most other primary malignancies (like kidney, breast, and lung) metastasize with osteolytic lesions, prostate cancer classically presents with osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone lesions [23, 24].

questions.question: Based on the clinical review sheets and correction tables in the sources, which legacy tumor marker is now considered obsolete for routine diagnosis or staging of prostate cancer, and which physical finding on DRE strongly differentiates BPH from prostate cancer?
options: Serum acid phosphatase is obsolete; on DRE, BPH feels smooth, firm, and elastic with a mobile rectal mucosa, while prostate cancer feels hard and irregular.
Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is obsolete; on DRE, BPH feels warm and fluctuant, while cancer feels soft and boggy.
Serum alkaline phosphatase is obsolete; on DRE, BPH feels nodular and fixed, while cancer feels symmetrically enlarged and elastic.
Urine cytology is obsolete; on DRE, BPH is completely non-palpable, while cancer presents with direct rectal wall ulceration.
questions.answerText: Serum acid phosphatase is obsolete; on DRE, BPH feels smooth, firm, and elastic with a mobile rectal mucosa, while prostate cancer feels hard and irregular.
questions.explanation: The sources explicitly highlight that serum acid phosphatase is an obsolete marker for routine diagnosis or staging of prostate cancer, having been replaced by PSA, pathology, and modern imaging [11, 15, 25]. On physical examination, DRE distinguishes BPH from cancer: BPH classically feels smooth, firm, and elastic (rubbery) with a symmetrically enlarged gland and a freely mobile rectal mucosa; whereas prostate cancer characteristically feels hard, irregular, and nodular with possible asymmetry or fixed overlying rectal wall [1, 20, 21, 26-29].

questions.question: What is the estimated prevalence of varicoceles in the general male population compared to those presenting with an abnormal semen analysis?
options: 5% in the general population; 15% in those with abnormal semen analysis
15% in the general population; 40% in those with abnormal semen analysis
40% in the general population; 15% in those with abnormal semen analysis
10% in the general population; 10% in those with abnormal semen analysis
questions.answerText: 15% in the general population; 40% in those with abnormal semen analysis
questions.explanation: According to the sources, varicoceles are present in 15% of all men, but this incidence increases to 40% in those with an abnormal semen analysis. They represent the most common correctable cause of male infertility.

questions.question: A clinician identifies an isolated right-sided varicocele during a physical examination of a 45-year-old male. Why does this clinical finding require urgent retroperitoneal imaging?
options: It is a normal anatomical variant that requires no further evaluation.
It suggests a left renal vein obstruction due to congenital absence of the vena cava.
It suggests retroperitoneal pathology, such as a renal cell carcinoma with an obstructing tumor thrombus in the vena cava.
It is highly associated with a patent processus vaginalis and a direct inguinal hernia.
questions.answerText: It suggests retroperitoneal pathology, such as a renal cell carcinoma with an obstructing tumor thrombus in the vena cava.
questions.explanation: An isolated right-sided varicocele is an important red flag. While left-sided varicoceles are common due to the drainage of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein, a right-sided varicocele is suggestive of retroperitoneal pathology, such as renal cell carcinoma with a tumor thrombus obstructing the inferior vena cava.

questions.question: For a male patient presenting with subfertility and a clinically palpable varicocele accompanied by an abnormal semen analysis, what is considered the best initial treatment of choice?
options: Long-term oral antioxidant therapy
Empirical Clomiphene citrate therapy
Microsurgical varicocelectomy
Immediate progression to IVF or ICSI directly
questions.answerText: Microsurgical varicocelectomy
questions.explanation: According to past exams and clinical target notes in the sources, the best initial treatment for a clinically significant varicocele with abnormal semen parameters and documented infertility is a microsurgical varicocelectomy.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presents with infertility. Semen analysis on two separate occasions confirms azoospermia. His testes are normal in size and consistency, and his serum hormone levels (testosterone, FSH, and LH) are all within normal limits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary seminiferous tubular failure
Klinefelter syndrome
Obstructive azoospermia
Secondary hypogonadism
questions.answerText: Obstructive azoospermia
questions.explanation: An azoospermic patient who presents with normal testicular size and normal FSH, LH, and testosterone levels is highly likely to have obstructive (post-testicular) azoospermia. In this scenario, a testicular biopsy is indicated to confirm normal spermatogenesis before reconstructive surgery or sperm retrieval.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man presents with infertility. He reports normal libido and erections. Semen analysis reveals a very low semen volume of 0.6 mL and azoospermia. His testosterone, FSH, and LH levels are completely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: Karyotyping
Post-ejaculatory urinalysis
Serum prolactin level
Diagnostic testicular biopsy
questions.answerText: Post-ejaculatory urinalysis
questions.explanation: When semen volume is extremely low (below 1.0 mL) in the context of azoospermia with normal hormone levels, retrograde ejaculation must be suspected. The initial screening investigation is a post-ejaculatory urinalysis to check for the presence of spermatozoa in the bladder.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man presents with infertility. On physical examination, he has small, firm testes and mild gynecomastia. Semen analysis confirms azoospermia. Serum biochemistry demonstrates a decreased testosterone level with markedly elevated FSH and LH. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Kallmann syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY)
Obstructive azoospermia
Prolactinoma
questions.answerText: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY)
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality (typically 47,XXY) characterized by primary hypogonadism, small firm testes, gynecomastia, azoospermia, and elevated gonadotropins (FSH and LH) with decreased testosterone.

questions.question: Serum tumor markers are essential in the diagnostic workup and staging of testicular germ cell tumors (GCTs). Which of the following statements correctly describes the marker profile of pure seminomas?
options: Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is markedly elevated in more than 90% of cases.
Both AFP and human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) are always normal.
Serum AFP remains uniformly normal, as any elevation in AFP indicates a non-seminomatous component.
hCG is raised in 100% of pure seminoma cases.
questions.answerText: Serum AFP remains uniformly normal, as any elevation in AFP indicates a non-seminomatous component.
questions.explanation: According to the sources, serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is never elevated (remains uniformly normal) in pure seminomas. If a patient with a suspected seminoma has an elevated AFP level, they are clinically managed as having a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents with a hard, painless, heavy right testicular mass that has been slowly enlarging. What is the definitive initial surgical management to establish a diagnosis and begin therapy?
options: Transscrotal percutaneous needle core biopsy of the mass
High (radical) inguinal orchidectomy
High-dose systemic combination chemotherapy with cisplatin followed by active surveillance
Transvesical retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND)
questions.answerText: High (radical) inguinal orchidectomy
questions.explanation: For any suspected testicular malignancy, a transscrotal biopsy is strictly avoided due to the risk of tumor seeding along the scrotal lymphatic pathways. Definitive management starts with a high (radical) inguinal orchidectomy.

questions.question: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is a well-established risk factor for developing testicular cancer. Which of the following statements is true regarding this association?
options: The risk is limited to the inguinal variety, whereas abdominal testes carry no increased risk.
The incidence of testicular malignancy is 15 times higher than the general population, with the intra-abdominal variety posing the highest risk.
Successful early childhood orchidopexy completely eliminates any future risk of testicular cancer.
Testicular cancer only occurs in the contralateral, normally descended testis.
questions.answerText: The incidence of testicular malignancy is 15 times higher than the general population, with the intra-abdominal variety posing the highest risk.
questions.explanation: Incompletely descended testes, particularly the intra-abdominal variety, carry a high risk of malignancy. The incidence of malignancy in an undescended testis is 15 times that of the normal population, and approximately 10% of patients with testicular tumors have a history of cryptorchidism.

questions.question: According to clinical findings and risk profiles described in the sources, what is the association between male subfertility and general cancer risk?
options: Infertile men have a significantly decreased risk of developing cancer compared to the general population.
There is no statistically significant correlation between male subfertility and cancer.
Infertile men have an increased risk of developing cancer compared to the general population, with the risk being highest in azoospermic men.
Only men with a history of bilateral cryptorchidism have an increased risk of cancer.
questions.answerText: Infertile men have an increased risk of developing cancer compared to the general population, with the risk being highest in azoospermic men.
questions.explanation: The sources explicitly note that infertile men have an increased risk of developing cancer compared to the general population. This risk is highest in patients with azoospermia.

questions.question: Penile fracture is a urological emergency that occurs due to blunt trauma to an erect penis. Which of the following represents the underlying pathology of this condition?
options: Rupture of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis
Tear in the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum
Complete transection of the urethra within the corpus spongiosum
Avulsion of the suspensory ligament of the penis
questions.answerText: Tear in the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum
questions.explanation: The sources state that trauma to an erect penis leads to penile fracture, which is pathologically defined as a tear in the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe penile pain, sudden detumescence, and a large hematoma ('eggplant deformity') following blunt trauma to his erect penis during sexual intercourse. What is the definitive management of this patient?
options: Application of a tight crepe bandage and outpatient follow-up
Plaster fixation and bed rest for 4 weeks
Urgent surgical exploration and repair of the tunica albuginea
Transurethral Foley catheterization and watchful waiting
questions.answerText: Urgent surgical exploration and repair of the tunica albuginea
questions.explanation: A penile fracture is a urological emergency that requires urgent surgical exploration and suture repair of the torn tunica albuginea to minimize long-term morbidity.

questions.question: During the clinical evaluation of a patient with a suspected penile fracture, which of the following clinical signs should strongly alert the clinician to investigate for a coexisting urethral injury?
options: Immediate detumescence and a 'rolling sign' over the hematoma
Blood at the urethral meatus or voiding difficulty
Severe suprapubic fullness and dullness to percussion
Presence of a unilateral inguinal hernia
questions.answerText: Blood at the urethral meatus or voiding difficulty
questions.explanation: A penile fracture can be associated with a urethral injury. Clinicians must suspect a coexisting urethral injury if there is blood at the meatus or voiding difficulty, and manage it accordingly.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the ER with an exquisitely painful, fully rigid penile erection of 15 hours duration. Penile blood gas analysis is performed. Which of the following blood gas profiles is characteristic of this patient's condition (Ischemic Low-Flow Priapism)?
options: Normoxic, normocarbic, and alkaline blood gases
Hypoxic, hypercarbic, and acidotic blood gases
Hyperoxic, hypocarbic, and neutral pH blood gases
Blood gases identical to systemic arterial blood
questions.answerText: Hypoxic, hypercarbic, and acidotic blood gases
questions.explanation: Ischemic (veno-occlusive, low-flow) priapism is a painful, rigid urological emergency characterized by little or no cavernous arterial inflow. Penile blood gas aspiration characteristically reveals hypoxic, hypercarbic, and acidotic blood gases.

questions.question: A clinician is evaluating a patient who presents with a prolonged, involuntary erection to differentiate between Ischemic (Low-Flow) and Non-Ischemic (High-Flow) Priapism. According to the sources, which of the following represents the most important diagnostic investigation?
options: Non-contrast spiral CT of the pelvis
Penile MRI with gadolinium enhancement
Coloured Duplex ultrasonography and penile blood gas analysis
Ascending voiding cystourethrography (VCUG)
questions.answerText: Coloured Duplex ultrasonography and penile blood gas analysis
questions.explanation: The sources designate 'Coloured Duplex - Penile blood gases' as the most important investigations for priapism to determine the type (ischemic low-flow vs. non-ischemic high-flow) and guide immediate emergency treatment.

questions.question: If ischemic (low-flow) priapism is neglected or treatment is significantly delayed, what is the primary long-term organic cause of subsequent erectile dysfunction?
options: Cavernous tissue fibrosis and failure of the cavernous veno-occlusive mechanism
Complete destruction of the pudendal nerve pathways
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to Leydig cell necrosis
Retrograde ejaculation due to bladder neck incompetence
questions.answerText: Cavernous tissue fibrosis and failure of the cavernous veno-occlusive mechanism
questions.explanation: Untreated ischemic priapism leads to prolonged hypoxia of the erectile tissue. Under the organic causes of erectile dysfunction, the sources highlight cavernous 'fibrosis (post-priapism)' as a primary venous/cavernous cause of permanent impotence.

questions.question: A 62-year-old male undergoes a radical prostatectomy for localized, high-grade prostate cancer. Postoperatively, he experiences severe erectile dysfunction. What is the primary anatomical and iatrogenic cause of organic erectile dysfunction following this procedure?
options: Complete division of both internal pudendal arteries
Injury to the cavernous nerves (neuropraxia/damage to the neurovascular bundles)
Severing of the suspensory ligament of the penis
Direct mechanical trauma to the corpus spongiosum
questions.answerText: Injury to the cavernous nerves (neuropraxia/damage to the neurovascular bundles)
questions.explanation: Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy is primarily caused by iatrogenic injury or neuropraxia to the cavernous nerves (neurovascular bundles) that travel in close proximity to the prostatic capsule.

questions.question: According to the surgical complications and past examinations in the sources, what is the most common sexual/ejaculatory complication that is inevitable after a radical prostatectomy?
options: Retrograde ejaculation
Hematospermia
Priapism
Premature ejaculation
questions.answerText: Retrograde ejaculation
questions.explanation: In the urology past exams section, a high-yield question asks for complications of prostate cancer, and lists 'Most common sexual complication after prostatectomy is retrograde ejaculation' as a true statement.

questions.question: A patient presenting with erectile dysfunction is being evaluated for potential drug-induced causes. According to the urological review sheets, which of the following drug classes is NOT typically associated with causing erectile dysfunction?
options: Sedatives
Antidepressants
Antihypertensives
Antifungals
questions.answerText: Antifungals
questions.explanation: According to the sources, medications that can impair male sexual function or cause erectile dysfunction include beta-blockers, thiazides, metoclopramide, sedatives, antidepressants, and antihypertensives.

questions.question: A 64-year-old male with long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral arterial disease presents with progressive, constant erectile dysfunction. No nocturnal erections are present. What is the most likely pathophysiological category of his organic erectile dysfunction?
options: Cavernous fibrosis post-priapism
Endocrine failure due to hyperprolactinemia
Mixed vascular insufficiency (atherosclerosis and microangiopathy) and diabetic neuropathy
Pure psychogenic anxiety
questions.answerText: Mixed vascular insufficiency (atherosclerosis and microangiopathy) and diabetic neuropathy
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus leads to mixed organic erectile dysfunction through multiple mechanisms: diabetic autonomic neuropathy, microangiopathy, atherosclerosis, and arterial insufficiency.

questions.question: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic to discuss her involuntary loss of urine. To help differentiate between Urgency Urinary Incontinence (UUI) and Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI), which of the following clinical features is most indicative of UUI?
options: Leaking of urine exclusively during physical activity such as running or coughing
The complete absence of nocturnal awakenings to pass urine
A sudden, strong, compelling desire to void that is accompanied by or immediately precedes the leakage
Immediate leakage of a few drops upon standing up from a chair with no prior warning
questions.answerText: A sudden, strong, compelling desire to void that is accompanied by or immediately precedes the leakage
questions.explanation: Urgency urinary incontinence (UUI) is defined as involuntary urinary leakage accompanied by or immediately preceded by urgency—a sudden, compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer [1-4]. Unlike SUI, UUI is also classically associated with daytime frequency (>8 times/24 hours) and nocturia (usually waking up to urinate at night), whereas SUI is seldom associated with nocturia or sudden urge episodes [5-7].

questions.question: Female Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI) typically results from pelvic floor dysfunction. Which of the following correctly pairs the underlying pathophysiology of SUI with its clinical description?
options: Urethral Hypermobility occurs when the pelvic floor muscles fail to support the bladder neck and urethra during abdominal pressure spikes; Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD) occurs when the sphincter is weak due to loss of the mucosal/submucosal sealing effect.
Urethral Hypermobility is caused by detrusor overactivity during bladder filling; Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency is caused by a suprasacral spinal cord injury.
Urethral Hypermobility refers to mechanical urethral strictures; Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency refers to uncoordinated relaxation of the levator ani muscles.
Urethral Hypermobility is treated primarily with antimuscarinic drugs; Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency is treated with intermittent catheterization.
questions.answerText: Urethral Hypermobility occurs when the pelvic floor muscles fail to support the bladder neck and urethra during abdominal pressure spikes; Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD) occurs when the sphincter is weak due to loss of the mucosal/submucosal sealing effect.
questions.explanation: SUI in women results from two primary anatomical and functional defects: (1) Urethral Hypermobility, where weakened pelvic floor muscles can no longer support the bladder neck and urethra, allowing them to descend and open during increases in intra-abdominal pressure; and (2) Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD), which is a intrinsic weakness of the urethral sphincter itself, caused by the loss of the sealing and mucosal/submucosal coaptation effect [8-10].

questions.question: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman complains of urinary leakage when coughing or sneezing. She has no pelvic organ prolapse. After she fails to improve with 3 months of supervised pelvic floor muscle exercises, she decides to undergo surgery. What is the gold-standard surgical treatment for her condition, and what is its mechanism?
options: Burch Colposuspension; it paralyzes the detrusor muscle to prevent sudden high-pressure storage.
Mid-Urethral Sling (TVT or TOT); it prevents posterior and inferior descent of the bladder neck and reinforces sub-urethral support during intra-abdominal pressure spikes.
Intradetrusor Botulinum toxin (Botox) injection; it physically blocks the urethral outlet to prevent leakage.
Artificial Urinary Sphincter; it is the universal first-line option for all typical female SUI cases.
questions.answerText: Mid-Urethral Sling (TVT or TOT); it prevents posterior and inferior descent of the bladder neck and reinforces sub-urethral support during intra-abdominal pressure spikes.
questions.explanation: When conservative measures like pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises fail for female SUI, surgery is considered [11, 12]. The gold standard is a mid-urethral sling—such as tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) or transobturator tape (TOT) [11, 13, 14]. These slings prevent the posterior and inferior descent of the bladder neck and reinforce sub-urethral vaginal support during periods of increased intra-abdominal pressure [15, 16]. Burch colposuspension is an alternative that elevates the paraurethral tissue adjacent to the bladder neck to the iliopectineal ligament [14, 17].

questions.question: A clinician is discussing non-surgical pharmacological options with a female patient suffering from mild stress urinary incontinence. Which of the following correctly states the physiological mechanism and key contraindication of oral/topical estrogen therapy for SUI?
options: Estrogens stimulate detrusor relaxation by blocking beta-3 adrenergic receptors; they are contraindicated in patients with severe uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.

Estrogens enhance the density and sensitivity of alpha-adrenergic receptors and exert trophic effects on the urethral mucosa; they are strictly contraindicated in women with a history of breast cancer.
Estrogens increase bladder capacity by directly inhibiting parasympathetic S2-4 pathways; they are contraindicated in patients with acute urinary retention.
Estrogens serve as a direct skeletal muscle relaxant for the levator ani; they are contraindicated in patients with a history of deep vein thrombosis.
questions.answerText: Estrogens enhance the density and sensitivity of alpha-adrenergic receptors and exert trophic effects on the urethral mucosa; they are strictly contraindicated in women with a history of breast cancer.
questions.explanation: Estrogen therapy can help female patients with SUI by enhancing the density and sensitivity of alpha-adrenergic receptors (which control internal sphincter tone) and by exerting trophic effects on the urethral mucosa, submucosa, and local collagen [18, 19]. However, because of the risk of stimulating hormone-sensitive malignancies, a history of breast cancer is a strict contraindication for estrogen therapy [18, 19].

questions.question: A 56-year-old female presents with symptoms of Overactive Bladder (OAB) accompanied by urgency urinary incontinence. Urinalysis is completely normal. Which of the following classes of medications is commonly used as first-line pharmacotherapy, and what is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Alpha-1 adrenergic blockers; they relax the bladder neck to reduce irritative storage symptoms.
Antimuscarinic agents; they inhibit bladder contractility (detrusor contractions), reduce sensory afferent input, and increase bladder capacity.
Loop diuretics; they promote rapid bladder emptying to avoid sudden urgency events.
Sympathomimetics; they stimulate the external urethral sphincter to remain tightly shut.
questions.answerText: Antimuscarinic agents; they inhibit bladder contractility (detrusor contractions), reduce sensory afferent input, and increase bladder capacity.
questions.explanation: The medical management of OAB and urgency urinary incontinence utilizes medications that inhibit involuntary detrusor contractions. Antimuscarinic agents (anticholinergics) are a mainstay of therapy; they work by inhibiting bladder contractility, reducing sensory (afferent) input to the CNS, and consequently increasing overall bladder capacity [10, 18]. Beta-3 adrenergic agonists (such as Mirabegron) are also a common option that facilitates bladder storage [20].

questions.question: A 58-year-old female patient presents with a combination of stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing or sneezing) and urgency urinary incontinence (leaking preceded by a sudden, intense urge). What is the recommended management strategy for Mixed Urinary Incontinence (MUI)?
options: Perform an immediate radical cystectomy and reconstruct an orthotopic neobladder.
Initiate high-dose systemic alpha-agonists and perform a Burch colposuspension simultaneously.
Direct treatment toward the most bothersome symptom first, utilizing a combination of bladder training and pelvic floor muscle exercises.
Treat the urgency component surgically and the stress component with continuous catheterization.
questions.answerText: Direct treatment toward the most bothersome symptom first, utilizing a combination of bladder training and pelvic floor muscle exercises.
questions.explanation: Mixed urinary incontinence (MUI) represents a combination of stress and urgency incontinence [3, 21]. The sources state that management of mixed incontinence should be directed toward the predominant or most bothersome symptom first [3, 21, 22]. Initial therapy typically combines conservative measures: bladder training (for the urgency component) plus pelvic floor muscle training (for the stress component) [22].

questions.question: A 68-year-old male with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with continuous dribbling of urine, a weak urinary stream, and nocturnal enuresis. On physical examination, a large, non-tender abdominal mass is palpable in his suprapubic region. A bedside ultrasound reveals a post-void residual (PVR) volume of 650 mL. What is the diagnosis, and what is the underlying pathophysiology?
options: Stress urinary incontinence; due to hypermobility of the prostatic urethra.
Urgency urinary incontinence; due to idiopathic detrusor overactivity.
Overflow incontinence; due to a decompensated, overdistended bladder secondary to chronic urinary retention (neurogenic detrusor weakness).
Total continuous incontinence; due to a newly formed prostatic-rectal fistula.
questions.answerText: Overflow incontinence; due to a decompensated, overdistended bladder secondary to chronic urinary retention (neurogenic detrusor weakness).
questions.explanation: Overflow incontinence is characterized by continuous involuntary loss of urine (often presenting as dribbling, weak stream, hesitancy, and nocturnal enuresis) resulting from mechanical forces on an overdistended bladder due to chronic urinary retention [21, 23, 24]. It is caused by bladder outlet obstruction or detrusor underactivity/weakness [21, 22]. In this diabetic patient, diabetic autonomic neuropathy has caused neurogenic detrusor weakness, leading to a high post-void residual (>300 mL) and subsequent overflow leakage [25-27].

questions.question: A 32-year-old female patient presents to the urology clinic complaining of total, continuous urinary incontinence (persistent leakage of urine with no normal storage) that began shortly after a long, difficult, and obstructed vaginal delivery. What is the most likely underlying cause of her incontinence?
options: Severe detrusor overactivity
Vesicovaginal fistula
Acquired intrinsic sphincter deficiency
Neurogenic bladder secondary to epidural anesthesia
questions.answerText: Vesicovaginal fistula
questions.explanation: Continuous or total incontinence is characterized by persistent leakage without normal bladder storage [21]. A classic cause of total urinary incontinence in females following an obstructed vaginal delivery is a vesicovaginal fistula (an abnormal epithelialized communication between the bladder and the vagina) [28-35]. Vesicovaginal fistula is the most common urinary fistula in women [13, 36]. Management requires anatomical localization and surgical reconstruction [22, 37].

questions.question: While stress urinary incontinence is highly common in women, it is relatively uncommon in the male population. According to the sources, in which clinical scenario does male stress urinary incontinence typically present?
options: In young men presenting with acute bacterial prostatitis and urethral discharge
In older men with severe untreated benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Following previous urethral surgery (e.g., radical prostatectomy) or pelvic irradiation
Following a simple laparoscopic cholecystectomy
questions.answerText: Following previous urethral surgery (e.g., radical prostatectomy) or pelvic irradiation
questions.explanation: Male stress urinary incontinence is uncommon [8, 10]. It typically only occurs if the male pelvic continence mechanisms (such as the external rhabdosphincter) have been damaged, classically following urethral or prostate surgery (such as radical prostatectomy) or pelvic irradiation [8, 10].

questions.question: A clinician is evaluating a patient with complex, recurrent urinary incontinence where the underlying mechanism remains uncertain. Which of the following diagnostic tools is considered the gold-standard functional test to measure bladder pressure, storage capability, and detrusor activity?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder (CT KUB)
Static 99mTc-DMSA renal cortical scintigraphy
Cystometry / pressure-flow studies (Urodynamic Study)
Rigid retroperitoneal laparoscopy
questions.answerText: Cystometry / pressure-flow studies (Urodynamic Study)
questions.explanation: While history, physical examination, and post-void residual (PVR) estimation are essential first steps [24, 38], invasive urodynamic studies (specifically cystometry and pressure-flow studies) are the gold-standard functional investigations to evaluate complex, recurrent, or neurogenic voiding dysfunction [39-41]. Cystometry measures the relationship between intravesical pressure, detrusor pressure, and bladder volume during filling and storage, helping to objectively identify detrusor overactivity, poor compliance, or sphincteric incompetence [12, 39-41].
